  • RAID 6: striping with double parity, usable capacity of (N-2)/N
  • RAID 10: stripe across mirrors, good performance with redundancy

Ubuntu commonly uses software RAID with mdadm.

Note

RAID 0 provides no fault tolerance. For SSD-backed arrays, RAID 1 or RAID 10 are usually preferred over RAID 5 or RAID 6 because of lower write amplification.

There are three broad RAID approaches:

  • Hardware RAID: handled by a dedicated controller
  • Software RAID: handled by the kernel and mdadm
  • Fake RAID: firmware-assisted RAID that depends on motherboard-specific metadata

Software RAID is the usual recommendation unless there is a clear need for a hardware controller.

docs.title: 5.3.1 Managing A Software RAID
docs.text:
mdadm is the standard tool used to create, assemble, inspect, and manage Linux software RAID arrays.

Common mdadm modes include:

  • Assemble: assemble an existing array
  • Build: build a legacy array without per-device superblocks
  • Create: create a new array with metadata on each member device
  • Manage: add, remove, or mark devices as failed
  • Misc: inspect or stop arrays and clear metadata
  • Monitor: watch arrays and trigger alerts
  • Grow: reshape or resize an array

The most common modern workflow is create.

# Examine RAID metadata on matching devices and save it to a file.
mdadm --examine /dev/vd[a-z]1 >> raid.status
Reference output 
No terminal output. The metadata is appended to raid.status.

Note

This example assumes virtio disk names such as vdb1 and vdc1. Adjust the device pattern for your environment, for example sd for SCSI/SATA or nvme for NVMe devices.

# Search the kernel log for messages related to virtio disks.
dmesg | grep vd
Reference output 
[    ... ] vdb: detected capacity change ...
[    ... ] vdc: detected capacity change ...

# Compare event counters across RAID member devices.
mdadm --examine /dev/vd[a-z] | egrep 'Event|/dev/'
Reference output 
/dev/vdb1:
    Events : ...
/dev/vdc1:
    Events : ...

# Attempt a forced assembly of an array.
mdadm --assemble --force /dev/mdX <list of devices>
Reference output 
mdadm: /dev/mdX has been started with ... drives.

/proc/mdstat shows the current RAID state from the kernel's point of view.

# Show the current software RAID status.
cat /proc/mdstat
Reference output 
Personalities : [raid1] [raid5] [raid6]
md0 : active raid5 vdb1[0] vdc1[1] vdd1[2] vde1[3] vdf1[4]
      ... blocks super 1.2 level 5 ... [5/5] [UUUUU]

unused devices: <none>

docs.title: 5.3.2 Software RAID Drive Failures
docs.text:
Two common RAID failure cases are:

  • resilience-reducing failures: the array is degraded but still works
  • operational failures: too many devices have failed and the array cannot run

Common array states include:

  • active
  • degraded
  • inactive
  • failed

When recovering a broken software RAID, start by preserving and inspecting the metadata before changing the array.

Important mdstat output elements:

  • [n/m]: expected devices versus currently active devices
  • [UUUU_]: U means the member is up; _ means a member is missing or failed
  • bitmap information: used to speed up resync after interruptions

Takeaway

For Linux software RAID, remember:

  • mdadm creates and manages the array
  • /proc/mdstat shows the kernel view of array health
  • RAID improves redundancy, performance, or both depending on the level
  • RAID is not a backup

docs.title: 5.4 RAID Lab
docs.text:
Info

Run this lab on LABVM. This workflow assumes /dev/vdb through /dev/vdf are available for testing.

docs.title: 5.4.1 Creating A RAID Setup
docs.text:
This lab uses mdadm to create and inspect a RAID 5 array.

Step 1: Install the required packages.

# Install mdadm and parted.
sudo apt install -y mdadm parted
Expected result 
Reading package lists... Done
Building dependency tree... Done
...
Setting up mdadm ...
Setting up parted ...

Step 2: Create GPT labels on the member disks.

# Create a GPT label on /dev/vdb (non-interactively).
sudo parted --script /dev/vdb mklabel gpt
Expected result 
No output.

# Create a GPT label on /dev/vdc (non-interactively).
sudo parted --script /dev/vdc mklabel gpt
Expected result 
No output.

# Create a GPT label on /dev/vdd (non-interactively).
sudo parted --script /dev/vdd mklabel gpt
Expected result 
No output.

# Create a GPT label on /dev/vde (non-interactively).
sudo parted --script /dev/vde mklabel gpt
Expected result 
No output.

# Create a GPT label on /dev/vdf (non-interactively).
sudo parted --script /dev/vdf mklabel gpt
Expected result 
No output.

Step 3: Create one partition on each disk.

# Create one full-disk partition on /dev/vdb (non-interactively).
sudo parted -a optimal /dev/vdb --script mkpart primary ext4 1MiB 100%
Expected result 
No output.

# Create one full-disk partition on /dev/vdc (non-interactively).
sudo parted -a optimal /dev/vdc --script mkpart primary ext4 1MiB 100%
Expected result 
No output.

# Create one full-disk partition on /dev/vdd (non-interactively).
sudo parted -a optimal /dev/vdd --script mkpart primary ext4 1MiB 100%
Expected result 
No output.

# Create one full-disk partition on /dev/vde (non-interactively).
sudo parted -a optimal /dev/vde --script mkpart primary ext4 1MiB 100%
Expected result 
No output.

# Create one full-disk partition on /dev/vdf (non-interactively).
sudo parted -a optimal /dev/vdf --script mkpart primary ext4 1MiB 100%
Expected result 
No output.

Note

The -a optimal option asks parted to align partitions using the device's preferred topology.

Step 4: Create the RAID 5 array.

# Create a RAID 5 array at /dev/md0 from the five member partitions.
sudo mdadm --create --verbose /dev/md0 --level=5 --raid-devices=5 /dev/vd[bcdef]1
Expected result 
mdadm: layout defaults to left-symmetric
mdadm: array /dev/md0 started.

Step 5: Watch the creation status.

# Watch the RAID creation progress.
watch cat /proc/mdstat
Expected result 
Every 2.0s: cat /proc/mdstat
... recovery = ...% (.../...)

Step 6: Check the current RAID status.

# Display the current RAID status.
cat /proc/mdstat
Expected result 
Personalities : [raid5]
md0 : active raid5 vdb1[0] vdc1[1] vdd1[2] vde1[3] vdf1[4]
      ... [5/5] [UUUUU]

Step 7: Examine the member metadata.

# Examine the RAID metadata on each member partition.
sudo mdadm --examine /dev/vd[b-f]1
Expected result 
/dev/vdb1:
    Magic : a92b4efc
    Version : 1.2
    Raid Level : raid5
    ...

Step 8: Show detailed array information.

# Display detailed information about /dev/md0.
sudo mdadm --detail /dev/md0
Expected result 
/dev/md0:
        Version : 1.2
  Creation Time : ...
     Raid Level : raid5
     Array Size : ...
     State : clean

Step 9: Search for related kernel messages.

# Search the kernel log for virtio disk messages.
sudo dmesg | grep vd
Expected result 
[    ... ] vdb: ...
[    ... ] md0: ...

Step 10: Open the mdadm manual for further tuning details.

# Open the mdadm manual page.
man mdadm
Expected result 
MDADM(8) ...

docs.title: 5.4.2 Removing A RAID
docs.text:
Removing a RAID array cleanly prevents mdadm from trying to reassemble it later from leftover metadata.

Step 1: Stop the array.

# Stop the active RAID array.
sudo mdadm --stop /dev/md0
Expected result 
mdadm: stopped /dev/md0

Step 2: Clear the superblock on /dev/vdb1.

# Remove RAID metadata from /dev/vdb1.
sudo mdadm --zero-superblock /dev/vdb1
Expected result 
No output.

# Remove RAID metadata from /dev/vdc1.
sudo mdadm --zero-superblock /dev/vdc1
Expected result 
No output.

# Remove RAID metadata from /dev/vdd1.
sudo mdadm --zero-superblock /dev/vdd1
Expected result 
No output.

# Remove RAID metadata from /dev/vde1.
sudo mdadm --zero-superblock /dev/vde1
Expected result 
No output.

# Remove RAID metadata from /dev/vdf1.
sudo mdadm --zero-superblock /dev/vdf1
Expected result 
No output.

Step 3: Check whether the array is referenced in mdadm.conf.

# Show ARRAY lines from the mdadm configuration.
grep ARRAY /etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf
Expected result 
ARRAY /dev/md0 metadata=1.2 UUID=...

Step 4: Edit the configuration file if needed.

# Edit the mdadm configuration file.
sudo nano /etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf
Expected result 
GNU nano ... /etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf

If an ARRAY entry for /dev/md0 is present, remove it or comment it out.

# Example alerting directive shown in mdadm.conf.
grep '^MAILADDR' /etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf
Expected result 
MAILADDR root

Takeaway

The practical RAID workflow is:

  • prepare the member disks
  • create the array with mdadm
  • monitor it with /proc/mdstat and mdadm --detail
  • when cleaning up, stop the array and clear leftover superblocks

docs.title: 5.5 Advanced LVM
docs.text:
LVM adds a management layer between block devices and the filesystems that use them.

Instead of working only with fixed partitions, LVM organizes storage in three layers:

  • physical volumes (PVs): disks or partitions prepared for LVM
  • volume groups (VGs): storage pools built from one or more PVs
  • logical volumes (LVs): named storage volumes created from a VG

This lets you treat several devices as one pool and carve out storage from that pool as needed.

Advantages of LVM:

  • named logical volumes instead of numbered partitions
  • logical volumes can span multiple disks
  • logical volumes do not need to be physically contiguous on disk
  • storage can be extended later with less disruption

LVM can also sit on top of software RAID. A common design is to build redundancy with mdadm first and then place LVM on the resulting RAID device.

It is usually a good idea to leave some free space in a VG so you can grow LVs later, create snapshots, or move data if the PV layout changes.

Basic LVM workflow:

# Initialize a disk as an LVM physical volume.
pvcreate /dev/vdx
Reference output 
Physical volume "/dev/vdx" successfully created.

# Create a volume group named my_vg.
vgcreate my_vg /dev/vdx
Reference output 
Volume group "my_vg" successfully created

# Create a 10 GB logical volume named my_lv.
lvcreate --name my_lv --size 10GB my_vg
Reference output 
Logical volume "my_lv" created.

Inspect the resulting PV, VG, and LV:

# Show the current physical volumes.
pvs
Reference output 
PV         VG    Fmt  Attr PSize   PFree
/dev/vdx   my_vg lvm2 a--  <...g   <...g

# Show the current volume groups.
vgs
Reference output 
VG    #PV #LV #SN Attr   VSize   VFree
my_vg   1   1   0 wz--n- <...g   <...g

# Show the current logical volumes.
lvs
Reference output 
LV    VG    Attr       LSize
my_lv my_vg -wi-a----- 10.00g

You can size an LV in bytes, MiB/GiB, extents, or percentages such as 20%FREE. LVM also supports different LV layouts including linear, striped, mirrored, and RAID-backed variants.

# Extend the volume group with another physical volume.
vgextend my_vg /dev/vdy
Reference output 
Volume group "my_vg" successfully extended

# Extend the logical volume by 20 GB.
lvextend -L +20GB /dev/my_vg/my_lv
Reference output 
Size of logical volume my_vg/my_lv changed from ... to ...

Note

lvextend increases the LV size only. If the LV already contains a filesystem, you usually need a separate filesystem resize step as well unless you use lvextend -r.

# Verify the updated VG free space and LV size.
vgs && lvs
Reference output 
VG    #PV #LV #SN Attr   VSize   VFree
my_vg   2   1   0 wz--n- <...g   <...g

LV    VG    Attr       LSize
my_lv my_vg -wi-a----- 30.00g

# Convert a linear LV into a mirror.
lvconvert -m +1 my_vg/my_lv
Reference output 
Logical volume my_vg/my_lv converted.

This requires enough free extents on another PV so LVM has somewhere to place the mirror image.

# Convert the mirrored LV back to linear.
lvconvert -m 0 my_vg/my_lv
Reference output 
Logical volume my_vg/my_lv converted.

# Move data away from a physical volume.
pvmove /dev/vdy
Reference output 
/dev/vdy: Moved: ...

# Move only the extents that belong to a specific logical volume.
pvmove -n my_lv /dev/vdx /dev/vdy
Reference output 
/dev/...: Moved: ...

Use pvmove when you need to evacuate a PV for maintenance or replacement. With -n, LVM moves only the extents that belong to the named logical volume.

# Show which physical volumes now hold the logical volume extents.
lvs -o +devices
Reference output 
LV    VG    Attr       LSize   Devices
my_lv my_vg -wi-a----- 30.00g /dev/vdy(...)

Takeaway

Keep the LVM layers straight:

  • PV = the disk or partition prepared for LVM
  • VG = the storage pool built from PVs
  • LV = the usable volume you create from the VG

Think of LVM as a flexible storage pool on top of block devices.

docs.title: 5.6 Advanced LVM Lab
docs.text:
Info

Run this lab on LABVM. This workflow uses /dev/vdb, /dev/vdc, and later /dev/vdd.

Step 1: Install LVM.

# Install the LVM tools.
sudo apt install -y lvm2
Expected result 
Reading package lists... Done
Building dependency tree... Done
...
Setting up lvm2 ...

Step 2: Create a GPT partition on /dev/vdb.

# Create a GPT label on /dev/vdb (non-interactively).
sudo parted --script /dev/vdb mklabel gpt
Expected result 
No output.

# Create one partition on /dev/vdb (non-interactively).
sudo parted --script /dev/vdb mkpart primary ext4 1MiB 100%
Expected result 
No output.

Step 3: Create a GPT partition on /dev/vdc.

# Create a GPT label on /dev/vdc (non-interactively).
sudo parted --script /dev/vdc mklabel gpt
Expected result 
No output.

# Create one partition on /dev/vdc (non-interactively).
sudo parted --script /dev/vdc mkpart primary ext4 1MiB 100%
Expected result 
No output.

Step 4: Create the physical volumes and list them.

# Create an LVM physical volume on /dev/vdb1.
sudo pvcreate /dev/vdb1
Expected result 
Physical volume "/dev/vdb1" successfully created.

# Create an LVM physical volume on /dev/vdc1.
sudo pvcreate /dev/vdc1
Expected result 
Physical volume "/dev/vdc1" successfully created.

# List physical volumes with backing device information.
sudo pvs -o +devices
Expected result 
PV         VG Fmt  Attr PSize  PFree  Devices
/dev/vdb1     lvm2 ---  ...    ...
/dev/vdc1     lvm2 ---  ...    ...

Note

On some systems, the Devices column may be empty at this stage even though the PVs were created successfully.

Step 5: Create the volume group and list it.

# Create a volume group named my_vg.
sudo vgcreate my_vg /dev/vdb1 /dev/vdc1
Expected result 
Volume group "my_vg" successfully created

# List volume groups.
sudo vgs
Expected result 
VG    #PV #LV #SN Attr   VSize  VFree
my_vg   2   0   0 wz--n- ...    ...

Step 6: Create the logical volume and list it.

# Create a 1 GB logical volume named my_lv.
sudo lvcreate -n my_lv -L 1GB my_vg
Expected result 
Logical volume "my_lv" created.

# List logical volumes.
sudo lvs
Expected result 
LV    VG    Attr       LSize
my_lv my_vg -wi-a----- 1.00g

Step 7: Prepare a filesystem for the later resize steps.

# Create an ext4 filesystem on the new logical volume.
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/my_vg/my_lv
Expected result 
mke2fs 1.47.0 (...)
Filesystem UUID: ...

# Create the mount point used in this lab.
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/data
Expected result 
No output.

# Mount the logical volume.
sudo mount /dev/my_vg/my_lv /mnt/data
Expected result 
No output.

Step 8: Convert the logical volume into a mirror.

# Convert my_lv into a mirrored logical volume.
sudo lvconvert -m +1 my_vg/my_lv
Expected result 
Are you sure you want to convert linear LV my_vg/my_lv to raid1 with 2 images enhancing resilience? [y/n]: y
Logical volume my_vg/my_lv successfully converted.

Step 9: Inspect the logical volume and physical volume usage.

# Show detailed information about the logical volume.
sudo lvdisplay /dev/my_vg/my_lv
Expected result 
--- Logical volume ---
LV Path                /dev/my_vg/my_lv
LV Name                my_lv
...

# Show physical volume usage.
sudo pvs
Expected result 
PV         VG    Fmt  Attr PSize PFree
/dev/vdb1  my_vg lvm2 a--  ...   ...
/dev/vdc1  my_vg lvm2 a--  ...   ...

Step 10: Convert the logical volume back to linear.

# Convert the mirrored LV back to a linear LV.
sudo lvconvert -m 0 my_vg/my_lv
Expected result 
Are you sure you want to convert raid1 LV my_vg/my_lv to type linear losing all resilience? [y/n]: y
Logical volume my_vg/my_lv successfully converted.

# Check physical volume usage again.
sudo pvs
Expected result 
PV         VG    Fmt  Attr PSize PFree
/dev/vdb1  my_vg lvm2 a--  ...   ...
/dev/vdc1  my_vg lvm2 a--  ...   ...

Step 11: Check which devices back the logical volume.

# Show logical volumes with backing device information.
sudo lvs -o +devices
Expected result 
LV    VG    Attr       LSize Devices
my_lv my_vg -wi-a----- 1.00g /dev/vdb1(...)

# Show detailed segment mapping for the logical volume.
sudo lvs --segments /dev/my_vg/my_lv
Expected result 
LV    VG    Attr       #Str Type   SSize
my_lv my_vg -wi-a-----    1 linear 1.00g

# Show how each physical volume is used.
sudo pvdisplay -m
Expected result 
--- Physical volume ---
PV Name               /dev/vdb1
...

# Show the block device view of the LVM layout.
sudo lsblk
Expected result 
NAME           MAJ:MIN RM  SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINTS
vdb            ...
└─vdb1         ...           part
  └─my_vg-my_lv ...         lvm  /mnt/data

Step 12: Move the logical volume to the other physical volume.

# Move my_lv from /dev/vdb1 to /dev/vdc1.
sudo pvmove -n my_lv /dev/vdb1 /dev/vdc1
Expected result 
/dev/vdb1: Moved: ...

Step 13: Verify that the move completed.

# Show the logical volume backing devices after pvmove.
sudo lvs -o +devices
Expected result 
LV    VG    Attr       LSize Devices
my_lv my_vg -wi-a----- 1.00g /dev/vdc1(...)

Step 14: Remove the now-free PV from the VG.

# Remove /dev/vdb1 from the volume group.
sudo vgreduce my_vg /dev/vdb1
Expected result 
Removed "/dev/vdb1" from volume group "my_vg"

Step 15: Extend the LV and resize the filesystem.

# Extend the logical volume by 1 GiB and grow the filesystem.
sudo lvextend -r -L +1G /dev/my_vg/my_lv
Expected result 
Size of logical volume my_vg/my_lv changed from 1.00 GiB to 2.00 GiB.
File system ext4 on /dev/mapper/my_vg-my_lv is mounted on /mnt/data; on-line resizing required
resize2fs ...

Step 16: Verify the larger filesystem and volume sizes.

# Check the mounted filesystem size.
df -h /mnt/data/
Expected result 
Filesystem               Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/mapper/my_vg-my_lv  2.0G  ...  ...   ...  /mnt/data

# List logical volumes after the resize.
sudo lvs
Expected result 
LV    VG    Attr       LSize
my_lv my_vg -wi-a----- 2.00g

# List volume groups after the resize.
sudo vgs
Expected result 
VG    #PV #LV #SN Attr   VSize VFree
my_vg   1   1   0 wz--n- ...   ...

Step 17: Prepare /dev/vdd and add it to the VG.

# Create a GPT label on /dev/vdd (non-interactively).
sudo parted --script /dev/vdd mklabel gpt
Expected result 
No output.

# Create one partition on /dev/vdd (non-interactively).
sudo parted --script /dev/vdd mkpart primary ext4 1MiB 100%
Expected result 
No output.

# Create an LVM physical volume on /dev/vdd1.
sudo pvcreate /dev/vdd1
Expected result 
Physical volume "/dev/vdd1" successfully created.

# Extend the volume group with /dev/vdd1.
sudo vgextend my_vg /dev/vdd1
Expected result 
Volume group "my_vg" successfully extended

# Check the updated volume group layout.
sudo vgs
Expected result 
VG    #PV #LV #SN Attr   VSize VFree
my_vg   2   1   0 wz--n- ...   ...

Step 18: Extend the LV again using the newly added space.

# Extend the logical volume by another 1 GiB and grow the filesystem.
sudo lvextend -r -L +1G /dev/my_vg/my_lv
Expected result 
Size of logical volume my_vg/my_lv changed from 2.00 GiB to 3.00 GiB.
resize2fs ...

# Verify the mounted filesystem size again.
df -h /mnt/data/
Expected result 
Filesystem               Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/mapper/my_vg-my_lv  3.0G  ...  ...   ...  /mnt/data

Step 19: Unmount the filesystem during cleanup.

# Unmount the logical volume from /mnt/data.
sudo umount /mnt/data
Expected result 
No output.

Step 20: Deactivate and remove the LVM objects.

Note

The commands in this cleanup step may prompt for confirmation depending on the current LV state.

# Deactivate the volume group.
sudo vgchange -an my_vg
Expected result 
0 logical volume(s) in volume group "my_vg" now active

# Remove the logical volume.
sudo lvremove my_vg/my_lv
Expected result 
Do you really want to remove logical volume my_vg/my_lv? [y/n]: y
Logical volume "my_lv" successfully removed.

# Remove the volume group.
sudo vgremove my_vg
Expected result 
Volume group "my_vg" successfully removed

# Remove the physical volume metadata.
sudo pvremove /dev/vdb1 /dev/vdc1 /dev/vdd1
Expected result 
Labels on physical volume "/dev/vdb1" successfully wiped.
Labels on physical volume "/dev/vdc1" successfully wiped.
Labels on physical volume "/dev/vdd1" successfully wiped.

Takeaway

The practical LVM workflow is:

  • create PVs
  • create a VG
  • create an LV
  • make a filesystem on the LV
  • extend the LV and filesystem as the VG grows

docs.title: 5.7 Device Mapper Multipathing
docs.text:
Device Mapper Multipathing (DM-Multipath) solves a specific storage problem: a server may be able to reach the same storage device through more than one physical path.

Those paths might go through different HBAs, cables, switches, or storage controllers, but they still lead to the same backend disk or LUN.

Without multipathing, Linux can show those paths as separate block devices even though they are not separate disks. That creates two risks:

  • you may mistake several paths for several independent disks
  • I/O may stop if the active path fails

DM-Multipath groups those paths into one logical device and keeps track of which physical paths belong together.

This provides:

  • path redundancy: fail over to another path if one path fails
  • improved performance: distribute I/O across multiple active paths when supported

Note

Multipathing solves path failure problems. It does not replace RAID. RAID protects against disk failure patterns, while multipath protects against path failure between the server and the storage.

Practical example:

  • a server is connected to the same SAN LUN through two Fibre Channel paths
  • Linux may see those paths as /dev/sda and /dev/sdb
  • without multipath, those names look like two disks even though they point to the same storage
  • with DM-Multipath, Linux exposes one logical device such as mpatha
  • if one path fails, I/O can continue through the remaining path

Student takeaway: when you see several devices with the same size and the same WWID, do not assume they are separate disks. They may just be separate paths to the same storage.

# Show the current block device layout.
lsblk
Reference output 
NAME   MAJ:MIN RM  SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINTS
sda      8:0    0  100G  0 disk
sdb      8:16   0  100G  0 disk

In a real multipath environment, entries like sda and sdb may be two paths to the same storage rather than two different disks.

# List multipath devices.
sudo multipath -ll
Reference output 
mpatha (3600508b400105e210000900000490000) dm-0 IBM,2810XIV
size=100G features='1 queue_if_no_path' hwhandler='0' wp=rw
|-+- policy='round-robin 0' prio=1 status=active
| `- 0:0:0:0 sda 8:0  active ready running
`-+- policy='round-robin 0' prio=1 status=enabled
  `- 1:0:0:0 sdb 8:16 active ready running

Note

In this VM-based lab, sudo multipath -ll may return no output because the guest does not have multiple paths to the same storage device.

DM-Multipath decides which paths belong together by using the device's WWID.

The WWID is the stable identity of the storage device. If device names change across reboots, the WWID still lets multipath recognize that the paths lead to the same backend storage.

# Display the WWID for a SCSI device.
sudo /lib/udev/scsi_id --whitelisted --device=/dev/sdX
Reference output 
3600508b400105e210000900000490000

Note

This WWID example applies to SCSI devices such as /dev/sdX. On virtio-backed VMs that use /dev/vdX, the command may return no output.

Takeaway

Multipathing means:

  • several device nodes may be several paths to the same storage
  • DM-Multipath groups those paths into one logical device
  • multipath protects against path failure, not disk failure

docs.title: 5.8 Device Mapper Multipathing Lab
docs.text:
Info

This lab is mostly a tool walkthrough. In a real environment, multipath is used with SAN or iSCSI storage that exposes multiple paths to the same LUN.

In this VM lab, the tools are present, but sudo multipath -ll may still show no devices because there is no true multipath storage backend.

Step 1: Install the multipath tools.

# Install the multipath tools.
sudo apt install -y multipath-tools
Expected result 
Reading package lists... Done
Building dependency tree... Done
...
Setting up multipath-tools ...

Step 2: Reload the multipath configuration and rescan devices.

# Reload multipath configuration and rescan for devices.
sudo multipath -r
Expected result 
No output.

Step 3: List the discovered multipath devices.

# Show the currently discovered multipath devices.
sudo multipath -ll
Expected result 
No output.

Takeaway

In this lab, the important point is:

  • the tools work even if the VM has no real multipath storage to show
  • in a real SAN environment, multipath -ll would group multiple physical paths under one logical device

docs.title: Virtualization
docs.text:
This chapter prepares the lab environment used in the rest of the course. Complete it before moving on.

In this chapter you will:

  • set up a QEMU and KVM lab VM
  • install Ubuntu in the guest
  • add storage and networking resources to the VM
  • use uvtool to create a VM from a cloud image

docs.title: 1.1 What Is Virtualization?
docs.text:
Virtualization lets one physical machine run multiple isolated guest systems. Each guest behaves like its own computer, with its own operating system, processes, and storage, while sharing the host's hardware resources.

Virtualization is different from emulation. Emulation recreates hardware in software and is usually slower. Virtualization uses hardware support from the CPU and kernel to run guests more efficiently.

On Ubuntu, the virtualization stack commonly includes QEMU, KVM, and libvirt.

You can use several commands to check whether a system is virtualized.

# Read SMBIOS and DMI data in a human-readable format.
sudo dmidecode
Reference output 
# dmidecode 3.5
Getting SMBIOS data from sysfs.
SMBIOS 2.8 present.

Handle 0x0000, DMI type 0, 24 bytes
BIOS Information
    Vendor: SeaBIOS
    Version: rel-1.16.2-0-gea1b7a073390-prebuilt.qemu.org

# Check kernel messages that may expose virtualization during boot.
sudo dmesg
Reference output 
[    0.000000] Hypervisor detected: KVM
[    0.058704] Booting paravirtualized kernel on KVM
[    2.430778] systemd[1]: Detected virtualization kvm.

# Detect the virtualization platform with a script-friendly systemd tool.
sudo systemd-detect-virt
Reference output 
kvm

# Identify the active virtualization platform with virt-what.
sudo virt-what
Reference output 
kvm

Takeaway

The main idea to remember is:

  • one host can run multiple isolated guests
  • KVM uses hardware acceleration
  • this is different from slower software-only emulation

docs.title: 1.2 KVM Virtualization Stack
docs.text:
KVM provides hardware-assisted virtualization in the Linux kernel. QEMU runs in userspace and provides the virtual hardware model that the guest sees. Used together, they let a guest run with near-native performance when the host supports virtualization extensions.

Libvirt provides a consistent management API and toolset. It manages guests, networks, storage pools, and device definitions on top of QEMU and KVM.

QEMU and KVM

QEMU can fully emulate a machine, but software emulation is slower. With KVM available, QEMU can execute guest code directly on the host CPU and use hardware acceleration.

When used together:

  • KVM handles CPU, memory, and hardware-assisted execution
  • QEMU emulates devices that the guest sees
  • libvirt manages guests, networks, storage pools, and device definitions

KVM

KVM is a kernel-based hypervisor that depends on CPU virtualization extensions. Ubuntu commonly uses it as the execution layer for virtual machines.

Common front ends are virsh for CLI management and virt-manager for GUI management. LXD can also manage VMs in newer environments.

QEMU

QEMU is the userspace component in the stack. It can run with KVM for hardware-assisted virtualization or fall back to software emulation through TCG when KVM is unavailable.

It also supports multiple CPU and hardware targets, which is why parts of QEMU are used across many virtualization solutions.

qemu-img

qemu-img creates, inspects, resizes, and converts disk images such as raw and qcow2.

# Inspect a disk image.
qemu-img info <image-file>
Reference output 
image: <image-file>
file format: qcow2
virtual size: 10 GiB (10737418240 bytes)
disk size: 200 KiB
cluster_size: 65536

libvirt

Libvirt provides a common API and toolset for virtualization management. In libvirt terminology, a VM is called a domain.

Before using libvirt with KVM, confirm that the host has the required virtualization features.

# Install the KVM capability checker.
sudo apt install -y cpu-checker
Reference output 
cpu-checker is already the newest version (0.7-1.3build2).
0 upgraded, 0 newly installed, 0 to remove and 0 not upgraded.

# Check whether KVM acceleration is available.
sudo kvm-ok
Reference output 
INFO: /dev/kvm exists
KVM acceleration can be used

You can also validate the host configuration more broadly with virt-host-validate.

# Validate the host for libvirt and QEMU use.
sudo virt-host-validate
Reference output 
QEMU: Checking for hardware virtualization                                 : PASS
QEMU: Checking if device /dev/kvm exists                                   : PASS
QEMU: Checking if device /dev/kvm is accessible                            : PASS
QEMU: Checking if IOMMU is enabled                                         : WARN

Libvirt includes virsh, which manages domains, networks, storage pools, and devices. These resources are defined in XML and can be exported, edited, or imported.

Warning

This lab expects the system libvirt connection. If virsh uri returns qemu:///session on your host, set export LIBVIRT_DEFAULT_URI=qemu:///system once before continuing. If you want that behavior to persist for future sessions, set uri_default = "qemu:///system" in ~/.config/libvirt/libvirt.conf.

# Use the system libvirt connection for the rest of the lab.
export LIBVIRT_DEFAULT_URI=qemu:///system

Takeaway

Remember the stack this way:

  • KVM runs the guest efficiently
  • QEMU provides the virtual hardware
  • libvirt with virsh manages the whole environment

docs.title: 1.3 Virtualization Lab
docs.text:
In this lab you will build LABVM on LABHOST using libvirt and virsh.

  • LABHOST: the host machine assigned to the student
  • LABVM: the guest VM created during the lab

docs.title: 1.3.1 Install A Guest VM
docs.text:
Start on LABHOST.

Info

This exercise prepares LABHOST to manage KVM guests with libvirt. Success means kvm-ok reports acceleration is available, the ubuntu user is added to the kvm and libvirt groups, and virsh list --all shows no domains yet.

Step 1: Update the host first.

# Refresh package metadata and upgrade installed packages.
sudo apt update -y && sudo apt dist-upgrade -y
Expected result 
69 packages can be upgraded. Run 'apt list --upgradable' to see them.
...
69 upgraded, 0 newly installed, 0 to remove and 0 not upgraded.
...
Running kernel version is 6.8.0-107-generic and it is up to date.
No services need to be restarted.

Step 2: Reboot the host.

# Reboot the host after package upgrades.
sudo reboot
Expected result 
Connection to 10.8.14.201 closed by remote host.
Connection to 10.8.14.201 closed.

After LABHOST finishes rebooting, log back in and continue with Step 3.

Step 3: Install the required virtualization packages.

# Install the QEMU, KVM, and libvirt toolchain.
sudo apt-get install -y qemu-system qemu-kvm libvirt-daemon libvirt-clients bridge-utils \
  libvirt-daemon-system qemu-utils cpu-checker virt-viewer virt-manager virtinst
Expected result 
0 upgraded, 257 newly installed, 0 to remove and 0 not upgraded.
...
Setting up qemu-system-x86 ...
Setting up libvirt-daemon-system ...
Setting up libvirt-clients ...
Setting up virtinst ...
Setting up virt-manager ...

Step 4: Verify that the host supports hardware virtualization.

# Confirm KVM acceleration is available.
sudo kvm-ok
Expected result 
INFO: /dev/kvm exists
KVM acceleration can be used

Step 5: Add the ubuntu user to the KVM-related groups.

# Add the ubuntu user to the kvm group.
sudo usermod -aG kvm ubuntu
Expected result 
No output.

# Add the ubuntu user to the libvirt group.
sudo usermod -aG libvirt ubuntu
Expected result 
No output.

Step 6: End the current session.

# End the current shell so group changes can take effect after re-login.
exit
Expected result 
No output.

Step 7: Log back in to LABHOST.

# Open a new SSH session to the lab host.
ssh ubuntu@<public IP>
Expected result 
Welcome to Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (GNU/Linux 6.8.0-107-generic x86_64)
ubuntu@playground-rdu:~$

Step 8: Confirm that no virtual machines exist yet.

Note

To make the rest of the lab easier to follow, set a custom shell prompt on LABHOST before you continue.

# Append a LABHOST prompt to ~/.bashrc.
printf '%s\n' 'PS1="\[\e[1;32m\]\u@LABHOST\[\e[0m\]:\[\e[1;34m\]\w\[\e[0m\]\\$ "' >> ~/.bashrc
Expected result 
No output.

# Reload ~/.bashrc in the current shell.
source ~/.bashrc
Expected result 
ubuntu@LABHOST:~$

# List all libvirt domains.
virsh list --all
Expected result 
 Id   Name   State
--------------------

An empty list is expected here because you have not created LABVM yet.

docs.title: 1.3.2 Set Up Storage Pools
docs.text:
Libvirt supports several storage back ends, including directory pools, filesystems, LVM, iSCSI, ZFS, RBD, and more. In this lab you will use a simple directory pool.

Info

This exercise creates the directory-backed storage pool used for VM disks. Success means vm-disks is active, Autostart is yes, and virsh pool-info vm-disks shows the pool details.

Step 1: Create the directory that will hold VM disk images.

# Create the directory-backed libvirt storage path.
sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks
Expected result 
No output.

Step 2: Define a storage pool that points to that directory.

# Define a new libvirt directory storage pool.
virsh pool-define-as --name vm-disks --type dir --target /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks
Expected result 
Pool vm-disks defined

Step 3: Check the pool state.

# List all storage pools.
virsh pool-list --all
Expected result 
 Name       State      Autostart
----------------------------------
 vm-disks   inactive   no

Step 4: Start the pool.

# Start the storage pool.
virsh pool-start vm-disks
Expected result 
Pool vm-disks started

Step 5: Enable pool autostart.

# Enable storage pool autostart.
virsh pool-autostart vm-disks
Expected result 
Pool vm-disks marked as autostarted

Step 6: Verify the pool again.

# Recheck the storage pool state.
virsh pool-list --all
Expected result 
 Name       State    Autostart
--------------------------------
 vm-disks   active   yes

Step 7: Review the pool details.

# Show detailed information for the storage pool.
virsh pool-info vm-disks
Expected result 
Name:           vm-disks
UUID:           cf41cccc-3ce1-4e5f-a0e1-31d06a0ca977
State:          running
Persistent:     yes
Autostart:      yes
Capacity:       97,87 GiB
Allocation:     8,40 GiB
Available:      89,47 GiB

docs.title: 1.3.3 Volume Operations
docs.text:
With the storage pool in place, you can create and manage volumes.

Info

This exercise shows how libvirt tracks virtual capacity separately from allocated disk usage. Success means sample-vol exists in the pool and later reports a resized capacity of 10 GiB.

Step 1: Create a qcow2 volume.

# Create a sparse qcow2 volume in the pool.
virsh vol-create-as vm-disks sample-vol 6G --format qcow2
Expected result 
Vol sample-vol created

By default, libvirt creates sparse files, so the allocated size on disk is much smaller than the virtual capacity.

Step 2: List the volumes in the pool.

# List volumes and their allocation details.
virsh vol-list --details vm-disks
Expected result 
 Name         Path                                   Type   Capacity   Allocation
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 sample-vol   /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/sample-vol   file   6,00 GiB   196,00 KiB

Step 3: Inspect the new volume.

# Show details for one storage volume.
virsh vol-info sample-vol vm-disks
Expected result 
Name:           sample-vol
Type:           file
Capacity:       6,00 GiB
Allocation:     196,00 KiB

Step 4: Resize the volume.

# Increase the virtual size of the volume.
virsh vol-resize sample-vol --pool vm-disks --capacity 10G
Expected result 
Size of volume 'sample-vol' successfully changed to 10G

Step 5: Confirm the new size.

# Verify the resized volume details.
virsh vol-info sample-vol vm-disks
Expected result 
Name:           sample-vol
Type:           file
Capacity:       10,00 GiB
Allocation:     200,00 KiB

docs.title: 1.3.4 Clone Volumes
docs.text:
You can clone a volume directly or use copy-on-write backing files.

Info

This exercise compares a full clone with a copy-on-write clone. Success means cloned-vol appears as an independent image and qemu-img info --backing-chain shows cow-clone using sample-vol as its backing file.

Step 1: Create a full clone.

# Clone the existing volume into a new file.
virsh vol-clone sample-vol cloned-vol vm-disks
Expected result 
Vol cloned-vol cloned from sample-vol

Step 2: Verify both volumes.

# List the pool volumes after cloning.
virsh vol-list --details vm-disks
Expected result 
 Name         Path                                   Type   Capacity    Allocation
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 cloned-vol   /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/cloned-vol   file   10,00 GiB   196,00 KiB
 sample-vol   /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/sample-vol   file   10,00 GiB   200,00 KiB

Step 3: Create a copy-on-write clone using the original as a backing file.

# Create a qcow2 copy-on-write image backed by sample-vol.
sudo qemu-img create -f qcow2 -b /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/sample-vol \
  -F qcow2 /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/cow-clone
Expected result 
Formatting '/var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/cow-clone', fmt=qcow2 cluster_size=65536 extended_l2=off compression_type=zlib size=10737418240 backing_file=/var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/sample-vol backing_fmt=qcow2 lazy_refcounts=off refcount_bits=16

Step 4: Inspect the backing chain.

# Inspect the qcow2 backing file chain.
sudo qemu-img info --backing-chain /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/cow-clone
Expected result 
image: /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/cow-clone
file format: qcow2
virtual size: 10 GiB (10737418240 bytes)
disk size: 196 KiB
backing file: /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/sample-vol
backing file format: qcow2
...
image: /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/sample-vol
file format: qcow2
virtual size: 10 GiB (10737418240 bytes)
disk size: 200 KiB

Warning

Do not attach the backing file itself to a VM in this scenario. Changing or booting the base image can corrupt all dependent copy-on-write images.

Step 5: Refresh the pool metadata.

# Refresh the pool after creating a disk outside virsh.
virsh pool-refresh vm-disks
Expected result 
Pool vm-disks refreshed

Step 6: Verify that the new image is visible to libvirt.

# List pool volumes after the refresh.
virsh vol-list --details vm-disks
Expected result 
 Name         Path                                   Type   Capacity    Allocation
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 cloned-vol   /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/cloned-vol   file   10,00 GiB   196,00 KiB
 cow-clone    /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/cow-clone    file   10,00 GiB   196,00 KiB
 sample-vol   /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/sample-vol   file   10,00 GiB   200,00 KiB

virsh pool-refresh is what makes the externally created cow-clone visible to libvirt.

Takeaway

Remember the difference:

  • a full clone is independent
  • a qcow2 copy-on-write clone saves space
  • a copy-on-write clone depends on its backing file staying unchanged

docs.title: 1.3.5 Libvirt Networks
docs.text:
Inspect the default libvirt network before creating a new one.

Info

This exercise identifies the default libvirt NAT network that already exists on LABHOST. Success means you can connect the default network to the virbr0 bridge and recognize the bridge address 192.168.122.1/24.

Step 1: List the active networks.

# List currently defined libvirt networks.
virsh net-list
Expected result 
 Name      State    Autostart   Persistent
--------------------------------------------
 default   active   yes         yes

Step 2: Inspect the default network.

# Show details for the default network.
virsh net-info default
Expected result 
Name:           default
UUID:           d2d78103-e29b-47cf-95be-e0e0d947e791
Active:         yes
Persistent:     yes
Autostart:      yes
Bridge:         virbr0

Step 3: Dump the network XML.

# Show the XML definition for the default network.
virsh net-dumpxml default
Expected result 
<network>
  <name>default</name>
  <uuid>d2d78103-e29b-47cf-95be-e0e0d947e791</uuid>
  <forward mode='nat'>
    <nat>
      <port start='1024' end='65535'/>
    </nat>
  </forward>
  <bridge name='virbr0' stp='on' delay='0'/>
  <ip address='192.168.122.1' netmask='255.255.255.0'>
    <dhcp>
      <range start='192.168.122.2' end='192.168.122.254'/>
    </dhcp>
  </ip>
</network>

Step 4: Inspect the bridge interface.

# Inspect the bridge backing the default libvirt network.
ip addr show virbr0
Expected result 
3: virbr0: <NO-CARRIER,BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP> mtu 1500 qdisc noqueue state DOWN group default qlen 1000
    link/ether 52:54:00:e1:87:2e brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
    inet 192.168.122.1/24 brd 192.168.122.255 scope global virbr0
       valid_lft forever preferred_lft forever

virbr0 can still show NO-CARRIER or state DOWN when no guest is attached. The main check here is that the bridge exists and holds the expected 192.168.122.1/24 address.

docs.title: 1.3.6 Define An Additional Libvirt Network
docs.text:
To define a custom NAT network, start with an XML definition.

Info

This exercise creates the custom nat-kvm-network network used later by LABVM. Success means libvirt starts the network, marks it for autostart, and creates nat-virbr2 with address 192.168.101.1/24.

Step 1: Inspect the network XML file.

# Review the custom libvirt network definition.
cat ~/nat-kvm-network.xml
Expected result 
<network>
    <name>nat-kvm-network</name>
    <forward mode='nat'>
        <nat>
            <port start='1024' end='65535'/>
        </nat>
    </forward>
    <bridge name='nat-virbr2'/>
    <ip address='192.168.101.1' netmask='255.255.255.0'>
    <dhcp>
        <range start='192.168.101.100' end='192.168.101.254'/>
    </dhcp>
    </ip>
</network>

Step 2: Define the network.

# Define the custom NAT network in libvirt.
virsh net-define ~/nat-kvm-network.xml
Expected result 
Network nat-kvm-network defined from /home/ubuntu/nat-kvm-network.xml

Step 3: Start the network.

# Start the custom libvirt network.
virsh net-start nat-kvm-network
Expected result 
Network nat-kvm-network started

Step 4: Enable autostart.

# Enable network autostart.
virsh net-autostart nat-kvm-network
Expected result 
Network nat-kvm-network marked as autostarted

Step 5: Verify the bridge address.

# Check the bridge address created for the new libvirt network.
ip addr sh nat-virbr2 | grep inet
Expected result 
    inet 192.168.101.1/24 brd 192.168.101.255 scope global nat-virbr2

Takeaway

In libvirt, a network is a managed resource:

  • you define it in XML
  • libvirt creates the bridge
  • libvirt applies the network behavior from that definition

docs.title: 1.3.7 Create The First VM
docs.text:
In this section, virt-install creates an Ubuntu 24.04 VM from a Canonical cloud image and connects it to the nat-kvm-network network.

The lab provides a helper script named create_vm.sh. Review it first.

Info

This exercise builds LABVM from a prepared cloud image and cloud-init ISO. Success means the ubuntu domain appears in libvirt and its definition shows the expected disk, CD-ROM, and network attachments.

Step 1: Inspect the VM creation script.

# Review the helper script that builds the VM.
cat create_vm.sh
Expected result 
#!/bin/bash

echo "Downloading the Ubuntu Noble image"
max_attempts=5
attempt=1
download_timeout=300  # 5 minutes

while [ $attempt -le $max_attempts ]; do
    echo "Download attempt $attempt of $max_attempts..."
    if sudo timeout $download_timeout wget -q --timeout 30 -O /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/ubuntu.img https://cloud-images.ubuntu.com/noble/current/noble-server-cloudimg-amd64.img; then
        if [ -s /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/ubuntu.img ]; then
            echo "Download successful!"
            break
        else
            echo "Download appeared successful but file is empty"
        fi
    else
        echo "Download attempt $attempt failed with status $?"
        if [ $attempt -eq $max_attempts ]; then
            echo "All download attempts failed. Exiting."
            exit 1
        fi
        echo "Waiting 30 seconds before retrying..."
        sleep 30
        attempt=$((attempt + 1))
    fi
done

echo "Resizing image"
sudo qemu-img resize /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/ubuntu.img +15G
echo "Copying cloud-init.iso"
sudo cp /home/ubuntu/cloud-init.iso /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/
echo "Changing ownership of new files"
sudo bash -c 'chown libvirt-qemu:kvm /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/*'

sudo virt-install \
    --name ubuntu \
    --ram 8192 \
    --vcpus 2 \
    --disk path=/var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/ubuntu.img,format=qcow2,bus=virtio \
    --disk path=/var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/cloud-init.iso,device=cdrom \
    --os-variant ubuntu24.04 \
    --network bridge=nat-virbr2,model=virtio \
    --graphics none \
    --console pty,target_type=serial \
    --import \
    --noautoconsole

The cloud-init.iso image provides initial configuration for the guest through user-data, meta-data, and network-config.

Step 2: Inspect user-data.

# Review the cloud-init user-data file.
cat user-data
Expected result 
#cloud-config
hostname: ubuntu

users:
  - name: ubuntu
    sudo: ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL
    groups: sudo
    shell: /bin/bash
    lock-passwd: false
chpasswd:
  list: |
    ubuntu:ubuntu
  expire: false
package_update: true
package_upgrade: true
package_reboot_if_required: true
packages:
  - vim
  - jq
  - qemu-utils
  - python3-swiftclient
  - libvirt-clients
  - git
  - openssh-server
  - sudo

growpart:
  mode: auto
  devices: ['/']
  ignore_growroot_disabled: false

resize_rootfs: true

ssh_pwauth: true

write_files:
  - path: /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-cloud-init.conf
    content: |
      PasswordAuthentication yes
      ChallengeResponseAuthentication no
      UsePAM yes
    append: true

runcmd:
  - systemctl restart ssh

Step 3: Inspect meta-data.

# Review the cloud-init meta-data file.
cat meta-data
Expected result 
instance-id: ubuntu-vm
local-hostname: ubuntu

Step 4: Inspect network-config.

# Review the cloud-init network configuration.
cat network-config
Expected result 
version: 2
ethernets:
  enp1s0:
    addresses:
      - 192.168.101.50/24
    nameservers:
      addresses:
        - 8.8.8.8
        - 1.1.1.1
    routes:
      - to: default
        via: 192.168.101.1
    renderer: networkd
    mtu: 1450

Step 5: Make the script executable.

# Make the helper script executable.
chmod +x ~/create_vm.sh
Expected result 
No output.

Step 6: Run the script.

# Create the Ubuntu VM from the cloud image.
~/create_vm.sh
Expected result 
Downloading the Ubuntu Noble image
Download attempt 1 of 5...
Download successful!
Resizing image
Image resized.
Copying cloud-init.iso
Changing ownership of new files

Starting install...
Creating domain...
Domain creation completed.

This step can take several minutes. The important success signal is Domain creation completed.

Step 7: List the defined VMs.

# List all domains after VM creation.
virsh list --all
Expected result 
 Id   Name     State
------------------------
 1    ubuntu   running

What matters most is that the ubuntu domain now exists. During the first boot, its state can change briefly while cloud-init finishes guest setup.

Step 8: Review the VM definition.

# Inspect the VM XML definition.
virsh dumpxml ubuntu | less
Expected result 
<domain type='kvm' id='1'>
  <name>ubuntu</name>
  <memory unit='KiB'>8388608</memory>
  <vcpu placement='static'>2</vcpu>
  ...
  <disk type='file' device='disk'>
    <source file='/var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/ubuntu.img' index='2'/>
    <target dev='vda' bus='virtio'/>
  </disk>
  <disk type='file' device='cdrom'>
    <source file='/var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/cloud-init.iso' index='1'/>
    <target dev='sda' bus='sata'/>
  </disk>
  ...
</domain>

docs.title: 1.3.8 Access The VM
docs.text:
After cloud-init finishes, the VM should have the ubuntu user and the configured static address.

Info

Run Steps 1 through 4 on LABHOST. Step 5 switches you into LABVM. Log in to LABVM with username ubuntu and password ubuntu. Success means the VM is set to autostart, responds to ping, and accepts an SSH login.

Step 1: Enable autostart for the VM.

# Configure the VM to start automatically with the host.
virsh autostart ubuntu
Expected result 
Domain 'ubuntu' marked as autostarted

Step 2: Confirm that the VM is running.

# List running domains.
virsh list
Expected result 
 Id   Name     State
------------------------
 1    ubuntu   running

Step 3: Open the serial console if needed.

# Connect to the VM serial console.
virsh console ubuntu
Expected result 
Connected to domain 'ubuntu'
Escape character is ^] (Ctrl + ])

ubuntu login:

If you open the console, leave it with Ctrl + ] before running the next command on LABHOST.

Step 4: Test network reachability.

# Verify that the guest responds on the lab network.
ping -c5 192.168.101.50
Expected result 
PING 192.168.101.50 (192.168.101.50) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 192.168.101.50: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.442 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.101.50: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=0.334 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.101.50: icmp_seq=3 ttl=64 time=0.431 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.101.50: icmp_seq=4 ttl=64 time=0.456 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.101.50: icmp_seq=5 ttl=64 time=0.309 ms

--- 192.168.101.50 ping statistics ---
5 packets transmitted, 5 received, 0% packet loss, time 4093ms
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 0.309/0.394/0.456/0.060 ms

Step 5: Log in to the guest.

# SSH into the guest VM.
ssh 192.168.101.50
Expected result 
ubuntu@192.168.101.50's password:
Welcome to Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (GNU/Linux 6.8.0-*-generic x86_64)
ubuntu@ubuntu:~$

Takeaway

After first boot, check both sides:

  • cloud-init handles the guest's initial setup
  • virsh confirms the VM exists and is running
  • ping, SSH, and the console confirm the guest is actually reachable

docs.title: 1.3.9 Attach Extra Disks To The VM
docs.text:
In this exercise, create several raw disks on LABHOST and attach them to LABVM.

Info

This exercise adds six extra disks that later storage labs will use. Success means LABVM shows new devices vdb through vdg in both /dev and lsblk.

Step 1: Return to the host.

# Exit the guest shell and return to LABHOST.
exit
Expected result 
logout
Connection to 192.168.101.50 closed.

Step 2: Create the raw disks.

# Create the first raw disk image.
sudo qemu-img create -f raw /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiskb.raw 10G
Expected result 
Formatting '/var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiskb.raw', fmt=raw size=10737418240

# Create the second raw disk image.
sudo qemu-img create -f raw /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiskc.raw 10G
Expected result 
Formatting '/var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiskc.raw', fmt=raw size=10737418240

# Create the third raw disk image.
sudo qemu-img create -f raw /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiskd.raw 10G
Expected result 
Formatting '/var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiskd.raw', fmt=raw size=10737418240

# Create the fourth raw disk image.
sudo qemu-img create -f raw /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiske.raw 10G
Expected result 
Formatting '/var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiske.raw', fmt=raw size=10737418240

# Create the fifth raw disk image.
sudo qemu-img create -f raw /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiskf.raw 10G
Expected result 
Formatting '/var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiskf.raw', fmt=raw size=10737418240

# Create the sixth raw disk image.
sudo qemu-img create -f raw /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiskg.raw 10G
Expected result 
Formatting '/var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiskg.raw', fmt=raw size=10737418240

Step 3: Refresh the pool and review the new volumes.

# Refresh the storage pool.
virsh pool-refresh vm-disks
Expected result 
Pool vm-disks refreshed

# List the pool volumes after the refresh.
virsh vol-list --details vm-disks
Expected result

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

 test-vmdiskb.raw   /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiskb.raw   file   10,00 GiB    4,00 KiB
 test-vmdiskc.raw   /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiskc.raw   file   10,00 GiB    4,00 KiB

 test-vmdiske.raw   /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiske.raw   file   10,00 GiB    4,00 KiB
 test-vmdiskf.raw   /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiskf.raw   file   10,00 GiB    4,00 KiB
 test-vmdiskg.raw   /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiskg.raw   file   10,00 GiB    4,00 KiB
 ubuntu.img         /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/ubuntu.img         file   18,50 GiB    1,85 GiB

Step 4: Attach the disks to the running VM.

# Attach the first raw disk to the guest.
virsh attach-disk ubuntu /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiskb.raw vdb --live --config
Expected result 
Disk attached successfully

# Attach the second raw disk to the guest.
virsh attach-disk ubuntu /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiskc.raw vdc --live --config
Expected result 
Disk attached successfully

# Attach the third raw disk to the guest.

Expected result

# Attach the fourth raw disk to the guest.
virsh attach-disk ubuntu /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiske.raw vde --live --config

virsh attach-disk ubuntu /var/lib/libvirt/vm-disks/test-vmdiskg.raw vdg --live --config

Disk attached successfully

After the attach commands succeed, wait a few seconds before reconnecting if the guest does not show the new devices immediately.

Step 5: Reconnect to the guest.

# Reconnect to the guest after attaching the disks.
ssh 192.168.101.50
Expected result 
ubuntu@192.168.101.50's password:
Welcome to Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (GNU/Linux 6.8.0-*-generic x86_64)

# List virtio block devices in the guest.

brw-rw---- 1 root disk 252, 48 ... /dev/vdd
